newsitem.title: POLAND: Clinton to share Poland's NATO joy, set out tasks.
newsitem.headline: Clinton to share Poland's NATO joy, set out tasks.

text.p: Poland's capital, festooned with huge U.S. embassy posters reading "President Clinton invites you," prepared to hold a street party with the American leader on Thursday in joy at the country's invitation to join NATO.

But Bill Clinton, arriving from NATO's Madrid summit, was also bringing a sober message that new members Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary will have to pay their share for security offered within the Western military alliance.
Clinton told the summit on Wednesday that he would talk in Warsaw of their responsibilities to make the pact stronger.
He pointed out that the entry of the three in 1999, a decade after they escaped Soviet domination, had yet to be ratified by legislatures of all 16 members including the United States.

Next year, the U.S. Senate will have to approve the enlargement and many influential Americans have doubts over the cost to U.S. taxpayers, the larger defence commitments, and the wisdom of antagonising Russia or undermining its democrats.

U.S. and Polish officials say that when Clinton speaks to celebrating crowds in the historic Castle Square -- rebuilt from ruins after World War Two -- the televised message will also show U.S. opinion the importance of the move.

"What President Clinton will say here, and the pictures of a Warsaw rebuilt from ruins which can now, like the whole of Poland enjoy effective guarantees of security, will be emotionally valuable for U.S. public opinion," Kwasniewski told public radio last month.
Clinton, who visited Poland in 1994 and heard its NATO case put by then president Lech Walesa, leader of the Solidarity union's 1980s defiance of communism, has backed Warsaw's entry.
Poland was completely dismembered from the 18th to early 20th centuries by its neighbours. It fell to German and Soviet invasion in 1939, effectively unaided by its Western allies.
After a heroic struggle on almost all fronts of World War Two, including Warsaw's 1944 uprising, it was reluctantly abandoned to Soviet control by London and Washington in 1945.
With this history, 80 percent of Poles want to join NATO and later the European Union.
While Clinton is talking with Kwasniewski and other Polish officials, Warsaw people will already be starting a jubilant five-hour party featuring jazz and folk music of both nations.
Clinton will not play his saxophone when he joins in to speak for 15 minutes, U.S. officials say.
Secretary of State Madeleine Albright and Foreign Minister Dariusz Rosati will discuss what Poland must do now, starting in August with complex negotiations with NATO.
Its tasks include making its unwieldy 230,000-strong forces compatabile with NATO's air control, command and communications standards -- likely to cost up to $3 billion over 15 years.
Poland must spend much more over this period modernising and re-equipping its forces, and is now working out how much it can afford without crippling its crucial economic growth.
It hopes for financial support from its allies and the best terms for its industry if it opts in future for arms such as the 100 modern multi-purpose fighters its forces want.
